“These thoughts soothed me, and that afternoon I fell deeply asleep. But the fever in my blood denied me peaceful dreams. The previous day’s terrible scene played endlessly before my eyes: the women fleeing, the furious Felix dragging me from his father’s feet. I woke exhausted. Seeing that night had already fallen, I slipped out of my hiding place to search for food.

“Once I had satisfied my hunger, I followed the familiar path toward the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crept into my shelter and waited silently for the hour when the family usually rose. That hour came and went. The sun climbed high in the sky, but none of them appeared. I shook violently, fearing some terrible misfortune. The cottage was dark inside, and I heard no movement. I cannot describe the anguish of that uncertainty.

“Before long, two countrymen passed by and stopped near the cottage to talk, gesturing vigorously. I could not understand them, because they spoke the local language, which was different from my protectors’ language. Soon afterward, however, Felix approached with another man. This surprised me, for I knew he had not left the cottage that morning. I listened anxiously, hoping their conversation would explain these unusual events.

“‘Do you realize,’ his companion said, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and give up everything your garden produces? I don’t want to take unfair advantage of you, so I beg you to spend a few days considering your decision.’

“‘There is absolutely no point,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the dreadful incident I have described. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. Please, don’t try to reason with me any further. Take back your property and let me escape this place.’

“Felix was trembling violently as he spoke. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed a few minutes, then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

“I spent the rest of that day in my shelter, utterly numb with despair. My protectors had gone, breaking the only bond that connected me to the world. For the first time, hatred and a hunger for revenge filled my heart. I made no effort to restrain them. Instead, I let their current carry me away and turned my thoughts toward violence and death.

With no work left in his hands, he pressed his right knuckles into his left palm, then his left knuckles into his right palm, then drew a hand across his bearded chin. He repeated these movements in a steady sequence without pausing for a moment. Bringing him back from the wandering state into which he always sank after speaking was like rousing an extremely weak person from a faint, or trying to hold back the departing spirit of a dying man in the hope that he might reveal something.

“Did you ask my name?”

“Yes, certainly.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

Making a weary sound that was neither a sigh nor a groan, he bent over his work again, until someone broke the silence once more.

“You aren’t a shoemaker by trade?” Mr. Lorry asked, watching him steadily.

His haunted eyes turned toward Defarge, as though he wanted him to answer. When no help came, they dropped to the floor before returning to the man who had asked the question.

“I’m not a shoemaker by trade? No, I wasn’t a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away for several minutes, his hands continuing their measured sequence all the while. At last his eyes slowly returned to the face they had left. As they settled on it, he started and resumed speaking like someone who had just woken and was returning to a subject discussed the night before.

“I asked permission to teach myself. It was very difficult, and I waited a long time before I got it. I’ve been making shoes ever since.”

He held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him. Still gazing steadily into his face, Mr. Lorry said:

“Monsieur Manette, don’t you remember anything about me?”

The shoe fell to the floor, and he sat staring at his questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry placed a hand on Defarge’s arm—“don’t you remember anything about this man? Look at him. Look at me. Doesn’t an old banker, an old business connection, an old servant, some earlier time come back to you, Monsieur Manette?”

As the man who had spent so many years in captivity stared from Mr. Lorry to Defarge, signs of a keen, attentive intelligence gradually emerged in the center of his forehead. Long erased, they struggled through the black fog that had engulfed him. The cloud covered them again; they faded and vanished. But they had been there.

“Story!”

He seemed deliberately to misunderstand the word she had echoed. He hurried on: “Yes, customers. In banking, we generally refer to our business contacts as customers. He was a French gentleman, a man of science and great learning—a doctor.”

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Yes, from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, this gentleman came from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, he had an excellent reputation in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our dealings were professional, though confidential. At the time, I was working in our French office and had been there for—oh, twenty years.”

“At the time—may I ask when you mean, sir?”

“I mean twenty years ago, miss. He married an Englishwoman, and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen and families, were managed entirely by Tellson’s. In the same way, I am, or have been, a trustee of one sort or another for scores of our customers. These are purely business relationships, miss. They involve no friendship, no personal interest, nothing resembling affection. Throughout my working life I’ve moved from one to another just as I move between customers during a working day. In short, I have no feelings; I’m simply a machine. To continue—”

“But you’re telling my father’s story, sir, and I’m beginning to think”—with that curious furrow in her forehead, she watched him intently—“that when I was orphaned, after my mother outlived my father by only two years, you were the person who brought me to England. I’m almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small hand she hesitantly offered in trust and raised it formally to his lips. Then he immediately guided the young woman back to her chair. Holding its back with his left hand, he alternately rubbed his chin, tugged his wig beside his ears, and emphasized his words with his right. He stood looking down into her face while she looked up into his.

“Miss Manette, it was me. And you’ll understand how accurately I described myself just now, when I said I had no feelings and that all my relationships with other people were purely business, if you consider that I’ve never seen you since. No; throughout that time you’ve been a ward of Tellson’s, while I’ve been occupied with Tellson’s other business. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. My entire life, miss, is spent turning the handle of an enormous financial wringer.”
